passages.title: Pods in CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled
passages.heading: Diagnosis
passages.content:
RB-K8S-001 · Pods in CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled · Diagnosis
1. `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n prod` and read Last State, Reason, and Exit
   Code. 137 = killed for memory (OOMKilled); 1 or 2 = application error.
2. `kubectl logs <pod> -n prod --previous` for the crash output, for example
   `KeyError: 'PAYMENTS_API_URL'` or `failed to parse config`.
3. Timing matters: OOMKilled within the first minute after start means the
   memory limit is too low for startup (or a config change raised usage). A pod
   that runs for hours and is OOMKilled after steady growth is a leak; see
   RB-APP-001.
4. Check what changed: `kubectl rollout history`, ConfigMap or Secret edits.

judge_reason: The passage explicitly instructs to run kubectl describe pod with the specific pod name and namespace to read the state, reason, and exit code.

passages.title: PostgreSQL disk full from WAL growth
passages.heading: Symptoms
passages.content:
RB-DB-003 · PostgreSQL disk full from WAL growth · Symptoms
orders-db data volume usage climbs steadily (alert `PgDataVolumeUsage > 80%`)
while table sizes are flat. Most of the growth is in `pg_wal/`. If the disk
fills, Postgres logs `PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.1234":
No space left on device` and the primary shuts down; every client then sees
"connection refused" on port 5432.

passages.title: PostgreSQL disk full from WAL growth
passages.heading: Diagnosis
passages.content:
RB-DB-003 · PostgreSQL disk full from WAL growth · Diagnosis
1. `du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/data/pg_wal` on the primary pod.
2. Find slots that pin WAL:
   `SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(),
   restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots;`
3. An inactive slot (`active = f`) retaining tens of GB is the usual cause,
   typically left behind by a decommissioned replica or reporting consumer.
4. Also check `archive_command` failures:
   `SELECT failed_count, last_failed_wal FROM pg_stat_archiver;`

judge_reason: The provided passages do not mention a specific replication slot named old_search_sync or the exact size of 112 GB.

passages.title: PostgreSQL disk full from WAL growth
passages.heading: Mitigation
passages.content:
RB-DB-003 · PostgreSQL disk full from WAL growth · Mitigation
- Confirm with the slot owner that the consumer is gone, then
  `SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('<slot_name>');`. WAL is recycled at the
  next checkpoint (`CHECKPOINT;` to force).
- If the disk is above 95%, expand the PVC first (`kubectl patch pvc
  data-orders-db-0 ...`); the storage class supports online expansion.
- Never delete files in `pg_wal/` by hand; it corrupts the cluster.
- Follow-up: set `max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB` so one slot cannot fill the disk.

judge_reason: The passages advise confirming with the slot owner and dropping the slot, but use a generic placeholder rather than the specific name 'legacy_reporting'.

passages.title: recommendations-api memory leak after v4.2.0
passages.heading: Summary
passages.content:
INC-2026-015 · recommendations-api memory leak after v4.2.0 · Summary
After v4.2.0 shipped on 2026-06-17, recommendations-api pods were OOMKilled
roughly every 3 hours for two days. During restarts the "You may also like"
widget was empty for about 6% of page views. Classified SEV3: a non-revenue
feature degraded; checkout and cart were unaffected.

passages.title: Memory leak after a deploy
passages.heading: Symptoms
passages.content:
RB-APP-001 · Memory leak after a deploy · Symptoms
After a new version ships, `container_memory_working_set_bytes` climbs in a
steady line instead of plateauing. Pods run normally for hours, then are
OOMKilled (exit code 137) and restart; the cycle repeats every few hours.
Latency worsens as pods approach the limit (more GC time), and brief error
bursts appear when several replicas restart close together.

passages.title: recommendations-api memory leak after v4.2.0
passages.heading: Root cause
passages.content:
INC-2026-015 · recommendations-api memory leak after v4.2.0 · Root cause
v4.2.0 added an in-process dictionary caching per-user feature vectors with no
size bound. Memory per pod grew linearly from 600Mi to the 2Gi limit, then the
kernel killed the container (exit code 137). The leak was confirmed by a
`tracemalloc` snapshot in staging showing the cache as the top allocator.
Startup memory was normal, which distinguished it from a too-low limit.

cart-api throwing errors on over half of requests, started 2 min ago.

2026-11-02T21:14:09Z ERROR cart-api  redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-cache:6379. Connection refused.
$ kubectl get pod redis-cache-0 -n prod
redis-cache-0  0/1  CrashLoopBackOff  3
Last State: Terminated  Reason: OOMKilled  Exit Code: 137
dashboard: cart-api error_rate=55%
claim: Redis memory exhaustion caused the Redis pod to be OOMKilled by Kubernetes, resulting in connection refused errors for cart-api.

passages.title: Redis memory exhaustion and eviction
passages.heading: Symptoms
passages.content:
RB-CACHE-001 · Redis memory exhaustion and eviction · Symptoms
redis-cache stores cart sessions for cart-api and short-lived price lookups for
checkout-api. When memory runs out, clients see one of:
- `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'` on writes (policy
  `noeviction`): cart updates fail, reads still work.
- A sudden rise in `evicted_keys` and cache misses (policy `allkeys-lru`):
  carts appear empty, latency rises from extra database reads.
- `Error 111 connecting to redis-cache:6379. Connection refused` if the Redis
  pod itself was OOMKilled by Kubernetes and is restarting.

passages.title: Redis memory exhaustion and eviction
passages.heading: Diagnosis
passages.content:
RB-CACHE-001 · Redis memory exhaustion and eviction · Diagnosis
1. `redis-cli -h redis-cache INFO memory` and compare `used_memory_human` with
   `maxmemory_human` (production: 6gb).
2. `redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys` to see eviction rate.
3. Find what grew: `redis-cli --bigkeys` and `redis-cli --memkeys`, and check
   for key prefixes written without a TTL (`OBJECT IDLETIME`, `TTL <key>`).
4. `kubectl -n prod describe pod redis-cache-0` and look for
   `Reason: OOMKilled`, which means the container limit is below maxmemory plus
   overhead.

passages.title: Pods in CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled
passages.heading: Symptoms
passages.content:
RB-K8S-001 · Pods in CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled · Symptoms
`kubectl get pods -n prod` shows `CrashLoopBackOff` with a rising RESTARTS
count, or `Reason: OOMKilled` / `Exit Code: 137` under Last State. Callers see
`connection refused`, `upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before
headers`, or 503 `no healthy upstream` when no ready endpoints remain. If only
some replicas crash, the error rate is partial.

judge_reason: The passages explicitly state that if the Redis pod is OOMKilled by Kubernetes, clients like cart-api see connection refused errors.

passages.title: TLS certificate expiry
passages.heading: Mitigation
passages.content:
RB-TLS-001 · TLS certificate expiry · Mitigation
- Force renewal: `cmctl renew <name> -n <ns>`, then confirm `READY=True` and
  restart pods that do not hot-reload certificates.
- If the issuer is broken, fix the `ClusterIssuer` secret first; renewal will
  not succeed until it reports `Ready`.
- Prevention: alert when any certificate expires in under 14 days
  (`certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds - time() < 1209600`).

passages.heading: Resolution and follow-ups
passages.content:
INC-2025-033 · Payments outage from expired card-vault mTLS certificate · Resolution and follow-ups
Fixed the issuer secret, ran `cmctl renew`, and restarted payments-api pods to
load the new certificate. Action item AI-455: alert on certificates expiring
in under 14 days. Action item AI-456: alert on any Certificate with
`READY=False` for more than 1 hour.

passages.title: Checkout outage from migration holding a table lock
passages.heading: Root cause
passages.content:
INC-2026-011 · Checkout outage from migration holding a table lock · Root cause
The release ran a migration `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders
(customer_id)` without `CONCURRENTLY`, taking a lock that blocked all writes
to `orders`. checkout-api requests waited on the lock, held their pool
connections, and new requests failed with `pool.acquire timed out after
5000ms`. orders-db had only 88 of 200 connections in use, so the first
responder's suspicion of connection exhaustion (INC-2025-014) was wrong;
`pg_stat_activity` showed 80 sessions with `wait_event_type = Lock`.

passages.title: PostgreSQL lock contention from long-running migrations
passages.heading: Symptoms
passages.content:
RB-DB-004 · PostgreSQL lock contention from long-running migrations · Symptoms
Application pools report acquire timeouts (for example "pool.acquire timed out
after 5000ms") and requests pile up, but orders-db is NOT near
max_connections: active connections are typically well under half of the 200
limit. Postgres logs `canceling statement due to lock timeout` or
`process 4121 still waiting for AccessExclusiveLock on relation 16402`. Onset
usually lines up with a schema migration or a manual `ALTER TABLE`.

judge_reason: The provided passages explicitly state that running the migration without CONCURRENTLY took a lock blocking writes, causing checkout-api requests to fail with pool acquire timeouts.

passages.title: Rolling back a bad deploy
passages.heading: When to roll back
passages.content:
RB-DEPLOY-001 · Rolling back a bad deploy · When to roll back
Roll back first and investigate second when error rate or latency rose within
about 30 minutes of a deploy and nothing else changed (no traffic spike, no
infrastructure change). Check the deploy log in #deploys or
`kubectl rollout history deployment/<service> -n prod`. If the deploy also
triggered a scale-out, check whether the scale-out is the real cause (for
example RB-DB-001) before assuming the code is at fault.

passages.title: Memory leak after a deploy
passages.heading: Diagnosis
passages.content:
RB-APP-001 · Memory leak after a deploy · Diagnosis
1. Overlay memory per pod with deploy markers; a leak shows a slope that starts
   at the deploy and resets on each restart.
2. Compare the same panel for the previous version; a flat profile there
   confirms the regression is in the new release.
3. For Python services, capture a live stack and allocation view with
   `py-spy dump --pid 1`, or enable `tracemalloc` snapshots via the
   `/debug/memory` endpoint in staging.
4. Usual suspects: unbounded in-process caches, per-request objects appended to
   module-level lists, or client sessions created per request and never closed.

v4.2.0 added an in-process dictionary caching per-user feature vectors with no
size bound. Memory per pod grew linearly from 600Mi to the 2Gi limit, then the
kernel killed the container (exit code 137). The leak was confirmed by a

passages.title: Unexpected 429s from ingress rate limiting
passages.heading: Symptoms
passages.content:
RB-NET-003 · Unexpected 429s from ingress rate limiting · Symptoms
Clients receive `429 Too Many Requests` from the ingress, not from the
application. ingress-nginx logs show `limiting requests, excess: 20.500 by zone
"checkout-api-rps", client: 203.0.113.10`. Application pods see lower traffic
than normal and their own error logs are quiet. Often follows a change to
`nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps` or to the CDN or proxy in front of the
ingress.

passages.title: Unexpected 429s from ingress rate limiting
passages.heading: Diagnosis
passages.content:
RB-NET-003 · Unexpected 429s from ingress rate limiting · Diagnosis
1. Check whether the limited `client` addresses are CDN or NAT egress IPs. If
   thousands of users share a few IPs, a per-IP limit throttles everyone.
2. `kubectl get ingress <service> -n prod -o yaml | grep limit` to read the
   current limit annotations.
3. Confirm the ingress trusts the forwarded client IP: `use-forwarded-headers`
   and `proxy-real-ip-cidr` in the ingress-nginx ConfigMap.
4. Rule out real abuse: a small number of distinct real client IPs with very
   high rates is an attack, not a misconfiguration.

INC-2026-015 · recommendations-api memory leak after v4.2.0 · Summary
After v4.2.0 shipped on 2026-06-17, recommendations-api pods were OOMKilled
roughly every 3 hours for two days. During restarts the "You may also like"
widget was empty for about 6% of page views. Classified SEV3: a non-revenue
feature degraded; checkout and cart were unaffected.
